document.title: Iranian Support to the Afghan Resistance
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan: Lessons from the Last War
document.note: DIA analyses from 1985 indicate that Iran and the U.S. both followed their separate interests in supporting the Afghan rebel movement, despite U.S. hostility toward Iran; may have implications for current parallel U.S. and Iranian statements on terrorism.

events.description: Overthrow of Zahir Shah; subsequent Iranian-Afghan agreements on Helmand waters and a rail link to Chah Bahar.
Khomeini revolution; Iranian Shiite clerics then began organizing Afghan Shiites in Hazarajat.
Iran supplied arms and equipment to Sunni Mujahedin in Pakistan including Hesb-e Islami.
Peshawar resistance recognized Iranian dominance over Hazara Shiite region; Iran thereafter severed ties with mainstream Peshawar groups.
Iranian arms shortages from offensives against Iraq limited material support to Afghan client groups.
Overthrow of Zahir Shah; Shah Pahlavi subsequently reaches agreements with Kabul on Helmand waters and a rail link to Chah Bahar.
Khomeini revolution; Iranian Shiite clerics soon begin organizing Afghan Shiites in the Hazarajat.
Iran supplies weapons and equipment to Hesb-e Islami while supporting Shiite groups in Hazarajat.
Iran severs ties with Peshawar-based resistance and deals almost exclusively with Afghan Shiite groups.
Weapons shortages from Iraq offensives limit Iranian material support to Afghan client groups from late 1983.

key_claims: Iran supported Sunni Hesb-e Islami with weapons from 1980 to mid-1982 but shifted almost exclusively to Afghan Shiite groups from mid-1983.
Iranian support to Shiite groups in the Hazarajat caused interfactional strife and weakened the overall resistance.
IRGC advisers in the Hazara region increased, increasing discipline and responsiveness to the Khomeini regime.
Material support was limited since late 1983 by weapons shortages from the war with Iraq.
About two million Afghans are in Iran, subject to repression, though some pro-Khomeini clerics unilaterally provided aid.
Iran's border crackdowns aim to avoid provoking Soviet retaliation, and Iranian and Soviet aims in Afghanistan risk collision.
Hazaras give Iran a bargaining chip over the future of the Kabul regime.
